case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Hogan v. Department of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: The court rejected separation-of-powers, vagueness and bill-of-attainder challenges to DCF's child abuse and neglect central registry scheme and held the hearing officer's decision to place the plaintiff's name on the registry was supported by the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Connecticut decision on the constitutionality of substantiation and central registry listing under § 17a-101k.
key_cases.quote: In sum, the trial court properly rejected the plaintiffs constitutional challenges to the registry scheme.

key_cases.case_name: Natasha B. v. Dept. of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: The Appellate Court held the hearing officer did not improperly shift the burden of proof to the plaintiff by scheduling a further hearing on whether changed conditions justified removing her name, and affirmed the substantiation and central registry placement.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Connecticut authority on burden allocation in the administrative hearing that follows a substantiated finding.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the hearing officer did not improperly shift the burden of proof to the plaintiff

key_cases.case_name: Matthew C. v. Commissioner of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: The Appellate Court held that the regulation permitting the department to rely on a prior judicial finding in a substantiation hearing requires that the respondent have had a full opportunity to be heard in the earlier proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Connecticut rule limiting when a court finding can substitute for an evidentiary hearing on substantiation.
key_cases.quote: we agree with the trial court that the regulation, like the doctrine of collateral estoppel, requires that there be a full opportunity for the respondent to be heard

key_cases.case_name: Daly v. Dept. of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: The Appellate Court affirmed dismissal of the administrative appeal, holding substantial evidence supported the hearing officer's substantiation of sexual abuse and the placement of the plaintiff's name on the central registry.
key_cases.relevance: This is the most recent published Connecticut appellate application of the substantial evidence standard to registry placement.
key_cases.quote: the hearing officer's determination that the department had satisfied the intent criterion for placement on the central registry was supported by substantial evidence

key_cases.case_name: Frank v. Department of Children & Families
key_cases.holding: The Appellate Court held that the statutory definition of a neglected child in § 46b-120(3) was unconstitutionally vague as applied to the plaintiff educator's conduct, invalidating the substantiation based on it.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Connecticut Appellate Court's vagueness limit on DCF substantiation under the emotional neglect definition.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that, under these facts, § 46b-120 (3) is unconstitutionally vague as to the plaintiff's conduct.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a suit against Connecticut child protection workers the Second Circuit held that investigators who have a reasonable basis for their substantiation determination do not violate the family's constitutional rights, and affirmed judgment for the defendants.
key_cases.relevance: It states the federal constitutional floor a Connecticut substantiation determination must satisfy.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that defendants had a reasonable basis for their substantiation determination and that they therefore did not violate plaintiffs' constitutional rights
